Project Title: A Unified Alabama Mesonet for Climate-, Fire-, and Weather-Related Decision Support

Project Benefits: This research will investigate the integration of Alabama's hydrometeorological observations into a mesonet, and in the process also discover new dataflows for research and decision-making. An improved data network will improve forecasts and save lives.

Project Title: Creating Digital Infrastructure to Expand the Healthy Air Network
Project Goal: To improve and expand the reach of life-saving air quality information across Massachusetts.
Project Description: This community driven project aims to expand the reach of life-saving air quality information across Massachusetts through the development of an app, website upgrades, and the addition of 20 air sensors through the Healthy Air Network. Updates to the website and developing the app will allow community members, decision-makers and stakeholders the ability to more easily access, utilize and analyze the hyperlocal data being collected on the site.
Project Benefits: As warming climate projections are expected to worsen air quality in communities, with already limited data available in Massachusetts, this project will provide the public with more accessible and actionable information on air pollution through development of an app and improved digital infrastructure. With this new infrastructure, residents can avoid outdoor time on high-risk air quality days, thereby avoiding direct health impacts. Increasing the number of sensors and towns will allow for increased accuracy of tracking the spatial and temporal variation of ozone at a finer resolution across the geographic area.

Project Title: Global GSB-Deployed Dropsondes and Mesh Networking
Project Goal: To develop the ability for Global Sounding Balloons to remotely deploy dropsondes while in flight to enable the collection of magnitudes more ins-situ data in areas of environmental interest.
Project Description: This project aims to develop the ability for Global Sounding Balloons (GSBs) to remotely deploy as many as 10 lightweight dropsondes while in flight. A GSB is a long-duration sensor-carrying balloon that collects and transmits real-time weather data throughout weeks-long flights. These dropsondes will carry a custom-built meteorological sensor suite similar to that which our GSBs are outfitted with and will communicate in-situ data back to their parent GSB in real-time via a closed radio network.
Project Benefits: A key component of improving weather prediction is a dramatic increase in available data. By equipping the WindBorne GSBs with as many as ten remotely deployed dropsondes per unit, this will enable NOAA and other leading industry partners to collect magnitudes more data in the most unreachable and high-risk environments without any additional risk to lives or property. This capability could mean hundreds of additional soundings of tropical cyclones, for example, and in turnmore accurate predictions for cyclone behavior. Importantly, the WindBorne GSB is relatively low cost, especially when compared to manned aircraft, and GSB dropsondes will also adhere to a sustainable cost model.

Project Title: Standardization, Calibration and Quality Control of Current and Emerging NOAA Aircraft Observations for Tropical Cyclone Analysis and Forecasting
Project Goal: By standardizing and reanalyzing aircraft observations and developing artificial intelligence surface wind reduction methods, this project aims to address observational gaps and improve tropical cyclone wind and storm surge guidance to support more accurate operational forecasts and warnings.
Research Keywords: Aircraft Reconnaissance, Artificial Intelligence (AI) / Machine Learning (ML), Radar, Satellite & Remote Sensing Technologies, Uncrewed Systems & Vehicles
Project Description: This project will create a standardized, single-format reanalysis database of Hurricane Hunter dropsondes and evaluate surface wind reduction methods using aircraft observations and Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System simulations. The project will develop machine learning models to estimate surface winds from non-standard observation heights, including data from small Uncrewed Aircraft Systems and Streamsondes. The resulting wind fields will be integrated into an experimental surface wind analysis system and evaluated as forcing for the operational SLOSH storm surge model. Optimized reconnaissance flight patterns will be developed and evaluated through real-time demonstrations and forecaster training in the Hurricane and Ocean Testbed.
Project Benefits: Improved understanding and AI techniques will be made with the dropsonde data, NOAA aircraft will be better utilized for the current and new technology. The public will benefit from improved watches and warnings for mitigation activities.

Project Title: Quality control of uncrewed observations and optimization of sampling strategies for improved tropical cyclone forecasts
Project Goal: Through developing an operational quality control framework and optimizing flight sampling strategies for small Uncrewed Aircraft Systems observations, this project aims to address observational data gaps in the tropical cyclone planetary boundary layer to improve numerical model predictions of hurricane track, intensity, and structure.
Research Keywords: Data Assimilation and Ensembles, Uncrewed Systems & Vehicles, Verification & Validation
Associated Forecast Systems & Models: Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation (GSI), Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System (HAFS)
Project Description: This project integrates small Uncrewed Aircraft System (sUAS) observations into the Hurricane Analysis and Forecast System Data Assimilation (HAFS-DA) system. The team will apply online quality control and observation error optimization techniques to sUAS observations collected during hurricane reconnaissance missions. Using both archival stepped-descent flight datasets and newly designed constant-altitude sampling strategies across the eyewall, inflow, moat, and rainband regions, numerical experiments will evaluate data impact on tropical cyclone forecasts. Finally, an optimized sUAS sampling configuration will be evaluated in a prototype real-time-equivalent demonstration within HAFS.
Project Benefits: Added value to existing data streams including a dedicated effort to add unique quality-controlled sUAS observations into HAFS-DA. The outcomes from this project will be directly transferred to NOAA's operational TC forecast modeling systems and Annual Hurricane Field Program.

Project Title: Advancing JEDI-Based Emission Inversion to Improve the NOAA Aerosols medium and long-range predictions
Project Goal: The primary goal of this project is to develop and implement novel machine learning (ML) methodologies within the Joint Effort for Data assimilation Integration (JEDI) framework to provide scalable emission adjustment capabilities to enhance global atmospheric composition predictions and subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) forecast skill.
Research Keywords: Atmospheric Composition and Chemistry, Coupled Models & Techniques, Data Assimilation and Ensembles
Associated Forecast Systems & Models: Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS), Unified Forecast System (UFS)
Project Description: This project advances the JEDI-UFS-GOCART system to bridge the gap between current emission estimation techniques and operational requirements. The research team will implement the JEDI Ensemble-Variational (EnVar) emission adjustment capability into the global system and deploy neural networks to emulate computationally expensive data assimilation components, such as concentration-to-emission Jacobians. Supported by a specialized one-year reanalysis to train these machine learning models, the project will ultimately deliver high-resolution, scalable emission updates for operational systems at a significantly reduced computational cost.
Project Benefits: Increases predictive lead times for global aerosol tracking across core NOAA systems, minimizes computational overhead burdens on operational processors via machine learning emulations, establishes transferable data assimilation capabilities applicable across distinct Earth system boundaries, and improves the reliability of public hazard management and safety warnings during severe wildfire events.

Project Title: Opportunities and Challenges (OCs) towards enhancing the prediction skill of US weather and climate extremes on the subseasonal range
Project Goal: The primary goal is to improve sub-seasonal (2-8 weeks) forecasting of weather and climate extremes in the United States by developing calibrated, probabilistic forecasts of year-round North American Weather Regimes (NAWR) and establishing physical links to surface extremes.
Research Keywords: Reanalysis & Reforecasting, Model & Forecast Guidance, Teleconnections
Associated Forecast Systems & Models: Global Ensemble Forecast System (GEFS), Unified Forecast System (UFS)
Project Description: This project identifies subseasonal "forecasts of opportunity" by bridging the gap between large-scale atmospheric patterns and local extreme events across the United States. The researchers will build an updated, year-round classification matrix of North American Weather Regimes (NAWR) and use the 30-year GEFSv13 hindcast archive to evaluate how effectively subseasonal models represent regime intensities, durations, and transitions. The final outcome will be a calibrated, probabilistic regime forecasting tool delivered directly to the NOAA Climate Prediction Center (CPC) to enhance operational subseasonal hazard guidance.
Project Benefits: Enhances reliable warning capabilities for destructive heatwaves and flooding, extends operational guidance from 2 weeks out to 3 weeks and beyond, and directly transfers diagnostic tools to CPC operations.
